newsitem.title: USA: Money pouring into battle for Congress hits record.
newsitem.headline: Money pouring into battle for Congress hits record.

text.p: Business, labour and individuals have poured a record $562 million into Senate and House election campaigns in the battle to control Congress, the Federal Election Commission reported on Friday.
As of Oct. 16, $300 million had gone to Republican candidates, $258 million to Democrats and $4 million to candidates in other parties, the commission said.

That does not include $46 million that organised labour and Republican and Democratic campaign committees are pumping into close races in excess of federal campaign laws, nor a vast fund of $54 million in "soft money" that campaign watch groups say is being used at least partly for congressional campaigns.
That additional money has triggered lawsuits, charges of buying Congress and calls for campaign finance reform laws.

President Bill Clinton, battered by allegations of improper campaign fund-raising, called on Friday for tighter laws requiring disclosure of money for political campaigns and voluntary spending limits for congressional candidates.
"It is time to change the rules," Clinton said.

Campaign analysts say many congressional races are so close Democrats could win back control of the House of Representatives and possibly even the Senate on Tuesday. Republicans won both in 1994 for the first time in 40 years.

The Federal Election Commission said the $562 million was contributed to candidates still campaigning for next Tuesday's elections. Including contributions to candidates who lost in primary elections, the total is $617 million, it said.

It said House Republican candidates were given $202.6 million of the $562 million and House Democratic candidates $168 million. Senate Republican candidates were given $97.1 million and Senate Democratic candidates $90 million.

The $562 million includes only the money contributed under federal campaign spending limit laws. In addition, the AFL-CIO labour organisation plans to spend $35 million primarily for television ads in 30 close House races in an effort to help Democrats win control. Republicans have filed lawsuits and accused labour of trying to buy control of Congress.

But labour has said it was taking advantage of the same federal court interpretation that Republican and Democratic campaign committees have utilized, which says campaign ads for or against candidates are not subject to federal limits unless they specifically ask for a vote for or against the candidate.

The National Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee this month has pumped $10 million in "independent expenditures" not subject to federal campaign limits into close Senate races. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has spent $1.1 million on such contributions.

That spending began after a divided Supreme Court ruled in June that political parties have a "free speech" right to spend campaign money without regard to spending limit laws -- so long as the funds are not coordinated with the campaigns, which are subject to the spending limits.

Democratic and Republican campaign committees have raised $54 million in "soft money," which is supposed to be used only for undefined "party building" activities or to help state and local -- but not federal -- candidates.

Campaign watch groups including the Centre for Responsive Politics say the party committees are using at least part of that money for television ads for or against Senate and House candidates. They claim they are not campaign ads because they do not specifically say to vote for or against a candidate.
